result:
If I could choose one small, ordinary thing to celebrate today, it would be windows.

Not grand cathedral windows or panoramic views from skyscrapers, but the humble windows of everyday life: the kitchen window fogged by boiling water, the bedroom window cracked open at night, the bus window streaked with rain, the office window that makes the hours feel survivable because there is light beyond the glass.

Windows are strange when you think about them. They are openings that are also barriers. They let you see the world without stepping into it. They frame reality like a painting, except the painting keeps changing: morning gold, gray noon, blue dusk, streetlamps glowing like little domestic stars.

Sometimes I imagine all the windows in the world as eyes. Apartments blinking awake at dawn. Shops staring out empty hours. Trains carrying moving gazes through stitched-together landscapes. Hospitals with windows that hold quiet prayers. Old houses with windows that have watched generations grow tall.

There is something comforting about seeing a lit window from far away, especially when you are walking home in the dark. It reminds you that ordinary life is happening everywhere. Someone is making tea. Someone is arguing. Someone is laughing at a video. Someone is crying. Someone is trying.

And then there are the moments when you stand at a window yourself. Looking out without really looking. Thinking the kind of thoughts that do not have words yet, only shapes. You watch a stranger pass below, and for one second you wonder about their entire life before they disappear around the corner. You see a bird lift from a wire. Clouds drift like slow thoughts. The world continues quietly on the other side of the glass.

Maybe that is why windows matter. They remind us that there is always something beyond where we are. Not necessarily something better. Just something else. Another room. Another street. Another sky. Another possibility.

So today, I would like to praise windows. The dirty ones, the clean ones, the cracked ones, the perfect ones. The ones that show us weather and time and distance. The ones that catch our reflection when we least expect it and make us look back at ourselves.

Because sometimes, in the middle of an ordinary day, all it takes is a square of light on a wall to remember that the world is still wide, still changing, still inviting us to look up.
